newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia Grain-Wheat in uncertain holding pattern.
newsitem.headline: Australia Grain-Wheat in uncertain holding pattern.

text.p: Australian grains markets settled into an uncertain holding pattern last week, waiting for more rain and undecided on the direction of future price movements.
Cash prices tracked Sydney Futures Exchange (SFE) futures prices, which rose over the week by about A$5.50 a tonne but ended the week on a slightly weakening note.

"Both Chicago and Sydney are completely weather dominated markets," Gary Booth of Ord Minnett Jardine Fleming Futures said on Friday. "Prices can be predicted only by those who can predict the weather."

Australia's wheat market responded to a mixed array of contrary influences over the week. These included reasonable local rain, which pushed prices down, uncertainty about whether more rain would fall, which pushed prices up, the certainty of looming tight supply, which also pushed prices up, and a weak market in the U.S., which dragged prices down.
Weakness in Friday's Sydney Futures Exchange wheat market indicated that the strongest influence eventually was possibly the USDA crop forecast during the week.

This pointed to 1997 U.S. wheat production of 2.531 billion bushels, well above expectations, and up on the government's July forecast of 2.431 billion and on analysts' average estimates of 2.476 billion.

"If we get reasonable rain in northern New South Wales (NSW) the SFE wheat market could possibly correct down by as much as A$10.00 a tonne to A$180.00. If that rain does not eventuate the market could push back above A$200.00 a tonne," Booth said.
This would compare with Friday's settlement close at A$194.50 a tonne by SFE market leader January 1998.
Australia's eastern and southern grain belt received fairly good falls of rain over the past week, at 10 mm to 25 mm, with some up to 50 mm, Bureau of Meteorology weathermaps show.
While this stabilised the domestic wheat market, in the words of the Australian Wheat Board (AWB), the industry agreed that more rain was still needed to guarantee the crop.
Farmers in the marginal lands of far western NSW were ploughing crops back in, Booth said.
"It's given good relief but they need more rain down south and they are certainly desperate for rain in the far west and the north," he said.
Wheat cash prices generally followed futures prices over the week. Cash sorghum was steady, while barley rose by about A$5.00 a tonne in northern NSW.
Bill Mitchell of New England Agricultural Traders described the week's cash trading as thin. Everything hinged on the weather watch, he said.

The threat by Western Australian grains growers to effectively secede from the rest of Australia's grains industry if it did not get a better deal on terms for the issue of shares in the privatising AWB provided the main spice in a week of continued grains market uncertainty.

The grains council of the Western Australian Farmers Federation (WAFF) said it had decided to recommend the WAFF withdraw from the peak national grains grower body, the Grains Council of Australia. This is expected to be ratified by an executive meeting of WAFF on August 20.

While the rest of the industry is treating the west's threat as real, a split is not seen likely to destroy the foundation of the Australian industry. The AWB's single desk monopoly on exports, which Western Australia wants split between east coast and west coast wheat, is regarded by the rest of the industry as a likely survivor of the row.
